title: Alexander H. Everett to Henry Clay, Madrid, 25 Sep 1825: three coded passages in the JQA code (catalogue 638)

documents.shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Despatches from US Ministers to Spain vol. 25, M31 reel 27 (naId 188610348), frames 0119-0121, enclosure 'Notes of a Conversation of Mr. Everett with Mr. Zea' (catalogue 638)

plaintext.source: Manning III (1925) doc. 1134 p. 2062 prints passage A as '[Here follow six lines in cipher, without decodification.]'; passages B and C are not printed.

transcription.notes: Contributed by WAINUT (27 Oct 2026). Three passages (A 8 lines, B 14, C 12), checked line by line against the frames a second time, independently. Measured with docs/_check_profile.py --measure --digits --drop-first.

system.summary: John Quincy Adams's numerical syllable-and-word code of 1811-1812 (the = 1385), about 1,600 numbers, rebuilt in ../jqa; used here unchanged.

system.notes: distinct_symbols = distinct groups in everett1825_transcription.txt (python docs/_check_profile.py --measure --digits --drop-first; 197 numbers, marked variants counted separately). Marks: lozenge = -s, caret = -ed, cross under 1535 = all and under 1167 = well, tick under a group truncates it.

prior_solution.where: Manning III (1925) doc. 1134 p. 2062 prints passage A undecoded and omits B and C; one web search found no decipherment. Not checked: another copy, a separate State Department file, the Clay Papers. A pencil note 'Decyphered' at the foot of MS p. 4 (frame 0114) suggests a decipherment was made in the Department; it was not found.

texts.label: Everett to Clay, Madrid, 25 Sep 1825 (catalogue 638), M31 reel 27 frames 0119-0121
texts.summary: Everett's notes of a conversation with the foreign minister Zea Bermudez on recognising the new American states: Zea's refusal is a language imposed on him by circumstances; the foreign ministers think him privately favourable but unable to risk his place against his rivals; the influence of Emperor Alexander is directed against recognition, and Russia's policy is put down to opposition to England rather than to legitimacy.

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 1 (M31-027-0112), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: Zea’s frankness may be natural to him, but he told Everett many things he could not believe himself – dissimulation, which public men must practise to some extent.

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 2 (M31-027-0113), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: Zea is said to have entered the cabinet through Ugarte, himself a creature of Russia; he soon broke with his patron and had him removed…

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 3 (M31-027-0113), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: … on a mission to Turin, though Zea himself is thought to be committed to Russian policy. Portrait: prepossessing, rather above middle height, robust but inelegant, bald, clear complexion, good teeth – rare in Spain, where most men, the King first, ruin theirs by smoking.

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 4 (M31-027-0114), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: He rolls his eyes so as to show the whites; tame face in silence, warm and frank in speech; a polished gentleman, fluent in French, at ease in English, less Spanish in air than any Spaniard Everett has met; liberal in conversation and abreast of the age, so that any illiberal notion he voices…

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 5 (M31-027-0114), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: … must be held for a purpose, against his real principles. Said to share the anticlerical prejudices of liberals; works days and several nights a week, rare among the King’s servants; a remarkable man among the prime ministers of Spain and Europe – if he is not soon overthrown…

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 6 (M31-027-0115), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: … by the strong rival party, he will vanish; if he lasts some years, his ministry will mark an epoch.

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 17 (M31-027-0120), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: The foreign ministers agree that Zea is personally favourable to recognition; a strong power must therefore act against it. He probably dares not risk his place, and if declaring for recognition would let his rivals…

texts.label: Everett, Notes of a conversation with Mr Zea, p. 18 (M31-027-0121), Brice Dudout
texts.summary: … overthrow him, he may think it wise to dissemble. Alexander I is said to oppose recognition; Everett has not yet spoken to d’Oubril. Some ministers ascribe Russia’s policy to opposition to England rather than to the legitimacy the Emperor professes.
